text.p: California's state Legislature ended its work for 1996 early Sunday. The following were the key bills passed as the session closed.
* Legislators approved a plan to open the state's massive electricity market to competition and slash consumer rates.

Initially, the utilities could issue, through the state infrastructure bank, about $5 billion in revenue bonds backed by a special transition charge. The utilities could issue additional "rate reduction bonds" later, for a total of $10 billion. The financings would provide savings to the utilities and those savings would be passed on to customers.
* Legislators gave final approval to measures creating a $10.5 billion agency that will sell earthquake insurance to homeowners in the state.

Under the complex plan that will fund the California Earthquake Authority (CEA), insurance companies that participate will provide the first non-reimbursable $1 billion in cash and will commit an additional $3 billion if needed to pay earthquake claims.
The CEA will purchase $2 billion in reinsurance and will be authorized to borrow an additional $1 billion.

Capital market investors would provide $1.5 billion to pay claims in excess of $7 billion, and if claims exceed $8.5 billion, the next $2 billion would be raised by another assessment on participating insurance companies.

If an earthquake produces more claims than available resources can handle, the California state Treasurer would be authorized to incur debt up to $1 billion, which would be repaid through assessments on CEA policyholders.

* Legislators approved a measure that would set up a state committee to advise financially troubled municipalities that may be considering bankruptcy. The bill would establish the Local Agency Bankruptcy Committee. Local governments would seek the committee's approval before filing for bankruptcy.

* Legislators approved a package of targeted tax cuts that would save businesses tens of millions of dollars over three years. The package of 24 tax cuts, totaling nearly $280 million over three years, will be offset by an accompanying set of 11 tax changes that should raise about $200 million during the same period, state officials said.
